conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I’ve had really high blood sugars all day. Around 5 PM, I got this tightness in my chest, right here in the middle, near my stomach. It scared me, so I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. Was the pain sharp or dull? Did it spread anywhere?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was more pressure than pain. Didn’t move anywhere. It went away after about 15 minutes, but my blood sugar was 706 when I checked after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s very high. We’ve confirmed it in the lab. You’re in diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA. That means your body is producing too many ketones because it doesn’t have enough insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve been taking my insulin. I don’t understand why this happened.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes even with good effort, blood sugars can spike. We’ll adjust your insulin while you’re here. Right now, we’re starting an IV insulin drip and giving you fluids to correct the imbalance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is the chest pain from my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your EKG and did blood tests for heart damage. Everything looks normal. The pain might be related to stress or acid in your blood from DKA. It’s not typical heart pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had it once before when I heard my son was in an accident. Same feeling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds like it could be anxiety-related. We’ll keep an eye on it, but no further heart testing is needed right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My back’s been hurting too. Can I get something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we gave you dilaudid earlier. You’re allergic to morphine and dilaudid, so we used a low dose carefully. We’ll switch to oral pain meds soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually take oxycodone from my regular doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart your oral oxycodone once you’re stable. For now, IV helps faster.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugar is coming down—now 382. Your anion gap is improving, which means the DKA is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Is my kidney okay? I remember last time they said I had kidney issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine was a bit high at 1.3, but it’s likely from dehydration. With fluids, it’s already improving. No long-term damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My heart rate’s still high, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s in the 110s, which is common in DKA. It should come down as you get more hydrated. EKG shows normal rhythm, no danger signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The endocrine team reviewed your case. We’re stopping the insulin drip and switching you to Lantus at night and Novolog before meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that different from what I was on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You were on 31 units of Lantus. Now it’s 33. And we’re giving you a sliding scale for Novolog to adjust based on your blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. Should I check more often?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, four times a day—before meals and at bedtime. We’ll teach you the scale before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are looking good. Anion gap is closed, blood sugar is stable. We’re moving you out of the ICU today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We want to make sure you’re managing your insulin well and your back pain is controlled on oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been constipated since I’ve been here. Is that from the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, oxycodone can cause that. We’ll start a stool softener and encourage fluids and movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been low-normal. We held your lisinopril at first, but we’re restarting it today since your kidneys are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take that every day. Was it unsafe to take with the DKA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In severe dehydration, it can affect kidney function. Now that you’re hydrated, it’s safe to restart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling a bit down lately. More than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know managing diabetes can be overwhelming. You’ve had over 20 DKA admissions. Have you had support for anxiety or depression?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see someone sometimes, but I’ve missed appointments. It’s hard to keep up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure your follow-up includes mental health support. It’s just as important as your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Blood sugars are in the 150–200 range. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Will I get more insulin to take home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll take Lantus 33 units at bedtime and Novolog with meals using the sliding scale we gave you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue aspirin, lisinopril, Zetia, and Protonix. We switched Protonix to pantoprazole—it’s the same type of medicine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about having another episode like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We all are. That’s why follow-up is crucial. Please see your diabetes doctor within a week. They’ll help fine-tune your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my back pain? I don’t have extra oxycodone at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We didn’t prescribe more. Please contact your primary doctor to refill it. We don’t restart narcotics at discharge without a review.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, or blood sugars over 350 or under 80.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ll make sure to keep my follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. Take care, and we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yeah. I brought my mom to the ER because she fell. Then I started feeling really tight in my chest and couldn’t catch my breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did the chest tightness come on suddenly? Was it worse with movement or breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started with gasping, then the chest tightness. It’s not worse when I breathe. I’ve had this before, usually when I’m stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any nausea or dizziness with it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, a little nausea. But no dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar was 551 when you arrived, and your labs show diabetic ketoacidosis. That means your body is under metabolic stress. We’ve started you on IV fluids and insulin to correct it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. I’ve been having high sugars the past couple days—mostly in the 300s. I haven’t been eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Poor intake can throw off your insulin balance. We’ll keep monitoring your levels closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take Lantus at night—31 units. I haven’t missed any doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. But we may need to adjust your sliding scale insulin. You’ve had DKA multiple times before—any idea why that keeps happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t know. Sometimes I just feel overwhelmed. I stopped taking Prozac a while back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be part of it. Depression and anxiety can make managing diabetes harder. We’ll recommend follow-up with a psychiatrist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess. I just don’t want to be on more meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But mental health is part of your overall care. Let’s focus on getting your sugars stable first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs show improvement. Glucose is down to 296, and your anion gap is closing. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My chest feels better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EKG and cardiac enzymes were normal, and your chest X-ray showed no issues. It looks like the chest tightness was related to stress or your metabolic state, not your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. It scares me every time it happens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll work on preventing these episodes by keeping your sugars more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I had a low sugar this morning—felt shaky around 5 AM.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood sugar was 68. It looks like your evening sliding scale insulin might be too high. We’re adjusting it—no more than 5 units at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I still take it if my sugar is high?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but capped at 5 units at bedtime. We’ll use Humalog now instead of Novolog, with a clear sliding scale.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue lisinopril for your kidneys, Zetia for cholesterol, and aspirin. Pantoprazole too, for stomach protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a yeast infection recently—just finished Diflucan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: High sugars can lead to that. Keeping your glucose under control will help prevent recurrences.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are looking good. Anion gap is normal, and your glucose is staying between 150 and 200.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Does that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. We want to make sure you’re stable and understand your insulin changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I want to do better. I just get so stressed sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important to recognize. We strongly recommend seeing a psychiatrist. Your depression may be affecting your diabetes care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it. Can I at least get a referral?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll set that up before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re clearing you to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What do I need to watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check your blood sugar before meals and at bedtime. If it’s over 400, call your doctor. If you feel shaky, sweaty, or confused, treat with juice or glucose tabs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel chest tightness again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it’s severe or you can’t eat or drink, come back. But try to stay calm—stress can trigger it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and follow up with your diabetes and mental health providers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve been really nauseous since this morning and I’ve thrown up a few times. I also have this cramping pain in my stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, diarrhea, or chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever or chest pain. I had one loose stool yesterday, but that’s it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You have type 1 diabetes—have you been able to keep your insulin up with not eating much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been trying, but I’m scared of going low. My sugars have been all over the place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll give you IV fluids and monitor your glucose closely. We also need to check for signs of ketoacidosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Is that what’s happening again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your initial labs show a slightly low bicarbonate but no big acid buildup yet. We’ll keep watching. You’re not in full DKA, but we’re seeing early signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not full DKA, but close?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re catching it early. IV fluids and careful insulin will help reverse it. We’ll also give you something for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling? Any vomiting since last night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous. I threw up once after coughing, but not on my own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s better than constant vomiting. Your labs this morning show your bicarbonate dropped to 17 and anion gap went up to 15—still mild, but we’re treating it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not severe, but it means your body is starting to burn fat for fuel. We’re correcting it with fluids and adjusting your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been compliant with my insulin, I swear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I believe you. Sometimes illness alone can throw things off, even if you’re doing everything right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start you on a liquid diet to see if you can keep things down. Still no fever or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, just the nausea and stomach cramps. Oh, and my back’s been killing me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned that. Where exactly is the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Middle of my back, on the left side. It’s been bad for years, ever since my car accident.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get an X-ray to make sure nothing’s changed. For now, we can try some acetaminophen and a lidocaine patch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually take oxycodone, but I ran out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re avoiding narcotics in the hospital because they can worsen nausea and aren’t great for long-term back pain. Let’s try safer options first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your back X-ray came back. Good news—it’s normal. No fractures or changes from before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing’s wrong with my spine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Structurally, no. The pain is likely muscular or related to old injury. We’ll keep using heat and the lidocaine patch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It helps a little, but I still need something stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll focus on non-narcotic options. Long-term, narcotics can make pain worse and aren’t safe with your other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your nausea is improving. You kept down apple juice and broth. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel queasy, but not like yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think this is viral gastroenteritis—your labs don’t show infection, and you don’t have fever. It should pass in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be gastroparesis? I’ve heard that happens with diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We considered that, but gastroparesis usually doesn’t come on suddenly, and you had diarrhea, which is less common with it. But you should get tested later if symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your blood work is improving. Bicarbonate is back to 20, no anion gap. You’re out of the early DKA phase.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! Does that mean I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. You need to keep down solid food and stay stable. We’ll try a soft diet today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my insulin? I’ve been so confused with the doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We lowered your Lantus to 15 units because you were having lows—down to 40s. You responded well to juice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate going low. It scares me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. We’ll send you home with clear instructions: 15 units tonight, then back to 31 tomorrow when you’re eating normally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my sliding scale?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using Humalog as before, but don’t take more than 5 units at night. We’re keeping that limit to prevent lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well today—kept down toast and applesauce. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue lisinopril, ezetimibe, aspirin, and your insulin. We’re adding compazine for nausea and ranitidine for heartburn.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for my back pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Acetaminophen and lidocaine patches. Use the patch for 12 hours, then off for 12. No narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess I’ll have to manage without them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. You’ve kept down a full meal. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When should I worry and come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If your blood sugar goes below 60 or above 350, or if you can’t keep food or liquids down. Also, chest pain or trouble breathing—go straight to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your primary doctor soon. We tried to schedule a mental health visit, but you’ve missed a few in the past?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know… anxiety makes it hard. But I’ll try this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. Managing stress helps your diabetes too. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel a lot better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. The nurse will go over your prescriptions and discharge instructions now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Patel. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I’ve been having nausea and vomiting for about five days now. It hasn’t gotten better, and my stomach hurts, especially when I throw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any diarrhea or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No diarrhea or fever. But some of my cousins had a stomach bug with diarrhea, so I think it might be something like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And your blood sugar—how has that been with all this vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been low. I haven’t been eating much, and I was still taking my usual insulin. I had a few lows at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll adjust your insulin while you’re not eating much. You were in the hospital a few days ago too, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but I left early because my grandfather passed away. I was feeling a bit better then and eating some food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry for your loss. It’s understandable you wanted to be with family. But coming back now means we should make sure nothing serious is going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m worried it’s not just a stomach bug. The pain and nausea won’t go away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your CT scan from earlier today. It shows no signs of appendicitis, blockage, or inflammation in the abdomen. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the nausea then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely, it’s a lingering viral gastroenteritis. Sometimes, if you start eating too soon or too much after being sick, it can flare symptoms again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I did try to eat a sandwich yesterday. Maybe that was too soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll start you on clear liquids and slowly advance your diet. We’ve also given you IV fluids to help with dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. What about my back pain? It’s been bothering me too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned a past car accident. The exam shows mild tenderness in your lower back muscles, but nothing urgent. We’ll manage it with acetaminophen for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on oxycodone before, but I’d rather avoid it if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. We’re using Dilaudid for breakthrough pain, but sparingly, especially since you have anxiety and we want to avoid sedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had panic attacks before. I don’t want to make that worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep that in mind. Now, your labs show your sodium was low when you arrived, but it’s improving with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mild hyponatremia like yours usually resolves with rehydration. We’re monitoring it closely, and it’s already getting better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. What about my diabetes? I’m scared of going into DKA again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood work doesn’t show signs of ketoacidosis this time. Your bicarbonate and anion gap are normal. That’s a big improvement from last admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. So I’m not in DKA now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you’re not. We’ve kept your Lantus insulin at a lower dose because you’re not eating much. That’s why you’ve had low sugars—we’re preventing more lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll go back to my regular dose when I eat normally?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll make sure you have clear instructions before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I kept down some apple juice and crackers last night. Nausea is less intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’re going to advance your diet to a full liquid, then soft foods today if you continue to do well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have some soup?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, broth-based soup is fine. Start small and let us know if you feel nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Oh, I heard something about a urine test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the first urine sample showed E. coli, but you have no symptoms of a UTI—no burning, urgency, or fever. We think it was contaminated, so we repeated it. The second test was normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We only treat if there are symptoms. No need to take antibiotics if you don’t have an active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. You’re tolerating regular food, your nausea is gone, and your labs are stable. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If nausea comes back, try to stay on clear liquids and don’t rush back to solid food. If you can’t keep fluids down, develop a fever over 101.4, or feel dizzy, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go back to your usual Lantus dose of 31 units at bedtime. Your Humalog sliding scale stays the same, but remember—no more than 5 units at night to avoid lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Should I see my doctor for follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please follow up with your primary care provider in a few days. If nausea persists, they might consider a gastric emptying study to check for gastroparesis, though it’s less likely given how fast this came on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make that appointment. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready, and a nurse will go over your medications before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need any new meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No new prescriptions. You’ll continue your usual ones: lisinopril, ezetimibe, aspirin, and pantoprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about adding more pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We keep things as simple as possible. Just focus on eating slowly, checking your blood sugar, and taking your insulin as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been having nausea and vomiting. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, chills, or abdominal pain besides the cramping with diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever or chills. Just the cramps. My blood sugars have been in the 200s, which is higher than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You were just discharged a few days ago for similar symptoms, right? Did you feel better before this came back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I was feeling fine after the last hospital stay. But two days ago, I saw my sister—she was sick with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. It sounds like you may have picked up a viral gastroenteritis from her. We checked your labs in the ER—your glucose was high at 339, but no signs of infection or kidney issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I feel so weak? And is my diabetes making this worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The weakness is likely from dehydration due to vomiting and diarrhea. Your diabetes doesn’t cause this, but it’s important we keep your blood sugar stable while you recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not nauseous right now, actually. I might even be able to eat something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll start you on clear liquids and see how you tolerate them. We also gave you some IV fluids to help with dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning look much better. Your electrolytes are stable, and your glucose is coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. I had some apple juice earlier and didn’t feel sick. Can I try solid food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll advance you to a light breakfast. If you tolerate that, you can have lunch too. Your body seems to be recovering well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done great—ate breakfast and lunch without any issues. No more diarrhea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel much better. Do I still need to stay here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you soon. Your medications haven’t changed—we’re sending you home with the same insulin and other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I watch for anything after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—call your doctor if nausea or vomiting returns, or if you have chest pain, trouble breathing, or can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugar? Should I check it more often?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep monitoring it as usual. Since your appetite is back, your insulin needs may return to normal. No changes to your sliding scale.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re just doing a quick blood draw to confirm your levels are stable before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s fine. I’m glad this passed quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Your labs are normal, and you’re tolerating food well. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll make sure to follow up with my regular doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Keep your appointments, stay hydrated, and take your meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Feel better, and take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ve been reviewing your case. You came in with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea—can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.text: I see. And your blood sugar was very high when you arrived—419. You hadn’t taken insulin that day, correct?

conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? I’ve had high sugars before, but never DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. The pain is better now, especially after the medication you gave me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember my clinic doctor suggested that. He also wanted me to get a colonoscopy and stool tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing this? It keeps happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will I have that done?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s scheduled soon—we’ll get you the details before discharge. For now, your symptoms are improving. You’ve been able to drink water and eat a little?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had some crackers and apple juice earlier. No vomiting since I got here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent progress. We’ll switch you to oral insulin soon. We’re also giving you loperamide for diarrhea as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And I should keep taking my regular meds—Lantus, Humalog, the others?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. All your home medications are continued, including ezetimibe, lansoprazole, and aspirin. Hyoscyamine is available for pain if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the dry rash I’ve had? It’s been spreading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. It doesn’t look infected, but it could be related to your diabetes or another skin condition. See your primary doctor for follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if your vitals stay stable and you continue tolerating food. Discharge is expected by midday. But return to the ER if you develop fever, blood in stool, or can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll be checking on you one more time before discharge. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’re feeling much better, still tolerating food, and ready to go home. Here’s your loperamide prescription and discharge instructions. Follow up with your doctor for the colonoscopy.

conversation_lines.text: I just couldn’t face it. I felt so nauseous and weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. That’s why we’re starting you on an insulin drip to bring your levels down safely, along with IV fluids to rehydrate you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My back’s been hurting too, worse when I’m stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you had a car accident in the past. We’ll manage your pain, but we want to avoid narcotics because they can worsen nausea and stomach issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my mom gives me her oxycodone sometimes. It helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it feels helpful, but using someone else’s medication is dangerous. It can lead to gastroparesis—where your stomach doesn’t empty properly—and make DKA more likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know that. I just want the pain to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess. But I just want to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get you there, but first you need to keep fluids down and your sugars stable. You haven’t been able to eat or drink much yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray came back normal—no pneumonia or other issues. Your EKG shows sinus tachycardia, which is common with DKA and dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it wasn’t a heart problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, your heart looks okay. The chest tightness was likely from anxiety and the DKA itself. Your breathing should improve as we treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your anion gap is starting to close, which means the DKA is resolving. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Still nauseous, but not vomiting as much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’re going to try giving you small sips of clear liquids. If you can keep those down, we’ll slowly increase your intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my insulin? I’m scared to mess up again.

conversation_lines.text: We’ll transition you back to your regular insulin—Lantus at night and Humalog as needed. But we’re lowering your Lantus dose to 25 units from 31.

conversation_lines.text: Why lower it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your body’s insulin needs can change, especially after stress. We don’t want you going low. You’ll resume your carb counting for Humalog.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The social worker came by. I didn’t say much. I’m just tired of talking about my feelings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But these repeated hospitalizations suggest we need to address the stress and depression. Your PCP can help connect you to mental health services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back negative for infection. The earlier mixed flora was likely contamination. Blood cultures also show no growth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I finished cipro for a UTI a few days ago. Could that have triggered this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Illnesses like UTIs can stress your body and raise blood sugar. But the bigger issue seems to be missing insulin when you’re unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just lose track when I feel bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. That’s why we do diabetes education—so you have a plan for sick days. We’ll go over that before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve kept down meals for two days, and your labs are stable. We’re stopping the IV fluids today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Does that mean I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: He’s been supportive. I think it’ll help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We also want you to follow up with your PCP within a week. They’ll help coordinate mental health support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Your nausea is gone, and your sugars are in a better range. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your Lantus at 25 units nightly. Use your Novolog pen for meals based on carbs. Keep eating regular meals and check your sugars four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel sick again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking insulin, even if you’re not eating. Drink fluids with sugar and electrolytes. If vomiting continues or you feel worse, come to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. We’ve given you prescriptions for your insulin, Tylenol, and a stool softener if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll try to do better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe in you. Take care of yourself, and don’t hesitate to reach out. Your health is worth it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We checked your blood sugar when you came in, and it was high. You also had a small acid buildup, which we call a modest anion gap. That’s common in uncontrolled diabetes. We’re starting IV fluids and insulin to help correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know my sugars have been high. I’ve been stressed. I’ve been using my mom’s pain pills to help with the stomach pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you're allergic to morphine, so we won’t use that. But we’ll manage your pain safely. We also ordered a CT scan to check your abdomen. It showed some thickening in the colon, but it looks stable and not acute.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? The colon thing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s been there a while, so it’s not an emergency. But we do need to check it further. The GI team recommends a sigmoidoscopy as an outpatient to make sure it’s not colitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. I was supposed to get a stomach test before, but I never went.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a gastric emptying study. That’s still important. Given your diabetes and ongoing nausea, we think you might have gastroparesis — that’s when the stomach doesn’t empty properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I feel full and sick all the time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And it’s common in people with long-standing diabetes. We’ll need that test to confirm. We also want a stool test for H. pylori, since you had it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I don’t want to stay in the hospital long. I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re focused on getting your blood sugar under control and keeping you hydrated. The nausea is improving with anti-nausea meds. But you’ll need to follow up on those tests after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are better today. The acid in your blood has cleared, and your sugars are coming down with the insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I still feel kind of shaky though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching that. It could be from the insulin or from not eating. We’re trying to get you to tolerate small sips. How’s your pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but not as bad. I’m just so anxious. I hate being in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The psychiatry team saw you yesterday. They think your anxiety is making things harder. They recommend starting mirtazapine at night for sleep and anxiety, and you can take Ativan up to three times a day as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on Celexa before. Did that help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They reviewed it and think it hasn’t been effective, so we’re stopping it. Mirtazapine might help more with both sleep and appetite.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine test came back. It showed mixed bacteria, but it’s likely contamination from skin or genital area, so we don’t think you have a UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. We’re focusing on your diabetes, stomach issues, and anxiety. Your blood pressure is a bit high too, but we’ll manage that with your regular meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. You’ve been off IV fluids since this morning and tolerating small amounts of food. Your pain is less, and you’re not vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d like to keep you a bit longer to finish monitoring, but we understand you want to leave. The GI team wanted to do the gastric emptying study and sigmoidoscopy here, but we can arrange them as outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d rather do them outside. I just can’t stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll set that up. But it’s very important you schedule them soon. Gastroparesis and colon changes need to be checked properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I promise I’ll call. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — your vitals are stable. You’ve been eating soft foods without vomiting. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue pantoprazole for stomach protection, ezetimibe for cholesterol, and your insulin. We’re adjusting your long-acting insulin to 8 units at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s lower than before. Why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your sugars were high but now are improving. We don’t want you going too low, especially if you’re not eating well. You’ll also take half a mirtazapine pill at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Ativan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one tablet up to three times a day for anxiety. But don’t take more than that. We also recommend following up with a psychiatrist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I need help. I’ve been struggling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Case management is helping set up appointments at Central Clinic. It might be easier for you to go to one place for all your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That would help. I get confused with all the different doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. Your discharge papers are ready. You’re stable, no fever, and you’ve been eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go. What do I need to do next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: First, call your GI doctor to schedule the gastric emptying study and sigmoidoscopy. They’re important to understand your stomach and colon issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call today. I mean it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Also, take your new meds as directed. Watch your blood sugar closely. If you start vomiting again or your sugars go very high, come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel really anxious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the Ativan as needed, but also try to reach your counselor. We’ve set up a case manager to help you stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll do better this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Take care, and please follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave — are you feeling okay to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m feeling much better. Still a little nervous, but I’ll be okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. Remember, the Ativan is there if you need it. And call the clinic if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge instructions are in your packet. The key points are: schedule the GI tests, take your meds, and follow up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve already called the GI office. They’re mailing me the prep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. Keep that momentum. You’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your insulin again before you leave. Make sure you’re comfortable with the doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I’ve got it. 8 units at night, and the fast-acting with meals based on my sugar and carbs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And use the sliding scale if your sugar is high. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — your A1c was high at 9.7%. We know diabetes is hard to manage, especially with everything else going on. But controlling it helps prevent complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I’ll try harder. I don’t want to lose my kidneys or go blind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re already taking steps. That’s what matters. We believe you can do this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay safe, and call if you need anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — you have a ride home and someone to check on you?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my sister’s picking me up and staying tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take it easy, and we’ll talk soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take these printed instructions with you. Call the clinic Monday to confirm your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee. You came in last night with abdominal pain and high blood sugar. Can you tell me how you’re feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m still having that crampy pain in my lower belly. It hasn’t gone away. And I was vomiting last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your blood sugar was very high—471—when you came in. We started you on an insulin drip to bring it down safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I took my glargine the night before, but it didn’t help. I don’t know why this keeps happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think this episode of diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA, may be due to not taking your insulin consistently. That can make sugars spike even if you take one dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I try, but sometimes I forget… or I feel anxious and just don’t do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. We’re here to help. Right now, your blood work shows an anion gap of 28, which confirms DKA. But we’re correcting it with fluids and insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, if not treated. But you’re in the right place. We’re watching you closely, and your levels are already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What about my stomach pain? It still hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your labs—lipase is normal, so it’s not pancreatitis. Your physical exam is benign—no tenderness, good bowel sounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be gastroparesis again? That’s what they thought last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re actually scheduling a gastric emptying study today to check that. It’s a test that tracks how fast food leaves your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I hope it shows something. I’m tired of being sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re also checking for infections. We did a urine test and cervical swabs to rule out STIs, since abdominal pain can sometimes come from there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t think it’s that, but okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Better safe. Your HCG came back negative, so you’re not pregnant, which is good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m on Depo-Provera, so that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your gastric emptying study came back. I have good news—your stomach is emptying normally. So it’s not gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait, really? But I feel so full and nauseous sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it feels real, and it is. But the test shows your stomach is working fine. Sometimes, with diabetes and anxiety, pain can be amplified even without a structural issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you’re saying it’s in my head?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. The pain is real. But it might be related to how your nervous system processes discomfort, especially when you’re anxious. That’s common in chronic conditions like diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been really stressed lately. And I hate being in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. Last admission, psychiatry suggested scheduled Ativan for anxiety. We’ve kept that—0.5 mg as needed, up to every 6 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It does help calm me down. But I don’t want to rely on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work with your mental health team on long-term strategies. For now, it’s okay to use it to stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your blood sugar is much better—145 this morning. We’ve transitioned you from the insulin drip to subcutaneous insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Does that mean I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your anion gap has closed, which means the DKA is resolving. Your kidneys were stressed on admission—creatinine was up—but it’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my kidney damage getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This was acute kidney injury, likely from dehydration. It’s not your chronic diabetic nephropathy getting worse. It’s already improving with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also stopped your ezetimibe. It’s for cholesterol, but it’s not urgent. We’ll restart it later if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine with me. I don’t even remember why I was on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. You’re doing well. Vital signs are stable. Heart rate is still a bit high—around 110—but not dangerous. It’s likely from anxiety and dehydration, both improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel jittery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring. Your EKG shows sinus tachycardia, but no heart damage. No fever, no infection found. MRSA screen and STI tests were negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the pain if not infection, gastroparesis, or kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t have a clear source. Your CT from last admission showed chronic colonic wall thickening, but no acute issue. Given all the normal tests, it may be related to your diabetes and anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So there’s nothing they can do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can help manage it. Continue your insulin, stay hydrated, and use Ativan as needed. We’re also referring you to GI and psychiatry for follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home today. Your blood sugar is stable, you’re eating and drinking, and your pain is better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I’m glad. But I’m scared it’ll happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can, if you don’t take your insulin. You must take your glargine every night—starting with 8 units at bedtime. We’re simplifying it to 5 units for now to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. But I forget sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please. If you don’t, you could end up back here with DKA. We’re giving you 30 Ativan tablets—take one every 6 hours as needed for anxiety, but not more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue pantoprazole and aspirin. Ezetimibe is stopped for now. Follow up with your doctor in a week to adjust insulin as you eat more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll do better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe in you. Call your doctor if sugars are high or pain returns. And please keep your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to come back here again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. You’re going home with clear instructions. You’re stronger than you think.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for not giving up on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Never. Take care. The nurse will go over discharge papers now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your urine culture showed some contamination, but also Gardnerella. That’s related to bacterial vaginosis. See your OB-GYN for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. I didn’t know. I’ll make an appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Stay well. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate it. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest and take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon, hopefully in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll try to make it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all for now. The nurse will help you get discharged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been vomiting and having diarrhea for three days. I couldn’t keep anything down, and I felt really weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you have type 1 diabetes—did you continue your insulin during this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I didn’t take it. I just didn’t feel like it. My son was sick too—gastroenteritis—and I thought I had the same thing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Not taking insulin during illness can lead to diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA. Your blood sugar was very high when you arrived—350 mg/dL.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I didn’t realize it could get that bad so fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can, especially when you're sick. We’ve started you on IV fluids and an insulin drip to correct the imbalance. We’ll monitor your levels closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been so anxious too. It’s hard to stay calm when I feel this bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I noticed you were very anxious in the ER. We’ve given you a dose of lorazepam to help. We’ll continue it as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My back also hurts—it’s been bothering me since my car accident a few years ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see that in your history. We’ll keep an eye on it. For now, your main issues are DKA and gastroenteritis, likely from the same bug your son had.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the vomiting and diarrhea aren’t from my diabetes directly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not exactly. The illness may have triggered the DKA, but the vomiting and diarrhea are likely viral. We checked your urine—no infection, and no ketones now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I was worried it was something worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also watching your kidneys. You have early diabetic nephropathy, so dehydration can affect them. But your labs are improving with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember my last admission—they said my kidneys were stressed. Is it the same this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, mild acute kidney injury, but it’s resolving. No need for dialysis. Just hydration and insulin are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I hate being in the ICU.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not in the ICU this time. You’re stable enough for the medical floor. We’ll keep you here for a few days to monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugar is coming down—171 now. We’ve stopped the insulin drip and given you a subcutaneous dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s better. I haven’t vomited since yesterday afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re adding metoclopramide—Reglan—to help with nausea and speed up stomach emptying, just in case there’s some gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Does that mean my stomach isn’t emptying right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but we don’t have proof right now. You’ve had repeated vomiting, so we’re being cautious. The medicine should help either way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about the brownish stuff I vomited? It looked like coffee grounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s concerning, but your rectal exam showed no blood, and your hemoglobin is stable. It’s likely a small tear from vomiting—called a Mallory-Weiss tear—or from esophagitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had esophagitis before. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not acutely. We’re keeping you on pantoprazole, your usual PPI, to protect your stomach lining. It should heal with time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ve also been feeling really down lately. The anxiety and depression just keep coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You’re on lorazepam for anxiety, and we’re increasing the dose slightly to help with withdrawal between doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to see my psychiatrist soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we recommend you follow up with them within the next few days. We’re sending you home with a short course of lorazepam to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are looking much better. The anion gap has closed, which means the DKA is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I start eating again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on clear liquids and advance as tolerated. Just remember to take your insulin with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I need to do better with that. It’s just hard when I’m sick or stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We get that. That’s why we’re also emphasizing follow-up with your primary doctor and psychiatrist. Support is key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve been off IV fluids since this morning, and your blood sugar is stable on your home insulin dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel more alert too. The lorazepam is helping with the anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’ll go home with metoclopramide for a few days and continue your regular meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my back pain? It’s still there, but not worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s chronic, related to your past accident. We didn’t see any new issues. Continue your usual care, and see your primary provider if it flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my A1C was 10.9%—that’s still too high, isn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it is. We recommend discussing tighter control with your endocrinologist. But for now, just focus on consistency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. We’re sending you with instructions and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll try to stick to my insulin this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. Take the metoclopramide three times a day for ten days. And keep taking the lorazepam as prescribed—don’t stop suddenly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call my psychiatrist tomorrow like you said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And if you vomit again, can’t keep insulin down, or feel confused, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. You’re going home in good shape—alert, walking, and stable. Just keep up with your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate everything you’ve done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still a little tired, but I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. Rest, stay hydrated, and take your meds. We’ll send the discharge papers shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge orders are ready. You’re officially cleared to leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call your doctors this week. You’ve got this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in one last time. Any questions before you leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Insulin, Reglan, PPI, and Ativan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And follow up with your team. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I heard you’re on your way out. Just wanted to say goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the cab’s here. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final note: your discharge diagnosis is DKA and gastroenteritis. Keep managing both.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be more careful next time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You're here because your blood sugar was extremely high and you’ve been feeling unwell. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been really anxious lately. My sugars were in the 200s this morning, but then they jumped to over 600. I’ve been thirsty, peeing a lot, and I’ve thrown up a few times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. We also saw you had some rectal bleeding in the ER. Did you notice that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I did have a few loose stools, but I didn’t see blood. I’ve had stomach issues before with my diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we know you have a history of gastroparesis. Right now, your labs show diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA. That means your body is producing too many ketones because it doesn’t have enough insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I missed a few insulin doses. I was so nauseous I didn’t eat, so I thought I didn’t need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a common mistake, but even when you’re not eating, your body still needs insulin. We’re starting an insulin drip to bring your levels down safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve been so dizzy and thirsty. Is that from the DKA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. DKA causes dehydration and high blood sugar, which leads to thirst, frequent urination, and nausea. We’re giving you IV fluids to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My back’s been hurting too. I usually take oxycodone, but I didn’t want to mix it with everything else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll manage your pain with safer options like Tylenol and ibuprofen. We’re avoiding narcotics unless absolutely necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugar has come down to 280, and your ketones are improving. We’re transitioning you from the insulin drip to subcutaneous insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I haven’t vomited since last night. Can I eat something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on a diabetic diet. Small, frequent meals are best. We’re also checking your thiamine levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thiamine? Why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because people with poor nutrition and chronic illness, especially with vomiting, can become deficient. We found yours was low, so we’re starting supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I haven’t been eating much. Thank you for catching that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an abdominal X-ray yesterday. It showed a lack of bowel gas, which is common in gastroparesis. No blockage, so that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I feel so full and nauseous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your stomach is emptying slowly. That’s why we’re holding off on metoclopramide for now — we want to see if your DKA improvement helps your stomach function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. My anxiety’s been worse too. I’ve been on sertraline, but it doesn’t feel like it’s helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry reviewed your case. They recommend increasing your sertraline to 100 mg daily. We’ll also keep your lorazepam for breakthrough anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try that. I just don’t want to keep ending up here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re setting you up with endocrinology and your psychiatrist after discharge. But we also need you to follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, but I’ve been overwhelmed. I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar spiked again last night, and your acid levels started to rise. We had to restart the insulin drip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so frustrated. I thought I was getting better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
