conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s the same as always—low back, doesn’t shoot down. I usually take my mom’s Percocet when it’s bad, but I don’t have any now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We’ll manage your pain here with safer options. Your blood work shows high glucose, ketones in your urine, and some acidosis—this suggests diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: DKA again? But I took my insulin. Why is this happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes even with proper insulin, stress—like pain or illness—can push your body into DKA. We’ll start an IV insulin drip and fluids to correct this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I be in the ICU?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, at least for the first 24 hours, so we can monitor you closely. Once your levels stabilize, we’ll move you to the regular floor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugar is coming down—now 220—and your acid levels are improving. We’re transitioning you off the insulin drip and back to your usual Lantus and Humalog.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I eat something? I’m really hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on a light diet. We also want to treat your nausea—so you’ll continue metoclopramide before meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that before. Does it help with gastroparesis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can help with delayed stomach emptying. But your prior tests showed normal emptying, so we think your nausea is more related to DKA and possibly stomach inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Inflammation? Like from that H. pylori infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re restarting treatment for H. pylori with two antibiotics and a stronger acid blocker for two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that last time. Do I really need it again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because if it’s not fully treated, it can keep causing stomach irritation and make diabetes harder to control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain team came by. They recommend starting acetaminophen and tramadol for your back pain, and a lidocaine patch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No stronger painkillers? I usually need something more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, we’re being cautious with opioids. These medications are safer and should help, especially with physical therapy later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess. But my back pain makes my blood sugar go up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s true—pain and stress do raise blood sugar. Managing your pain well will help your diabetes too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are looking much better. Blood sugar is stable, and your kidney function has improved. We’re planning to move you out of the ICU today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Does that mean I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re doing well. Your vitals are stable, and you’re eating without vomiting. We just need to make sure your insulin doses keep your sugars in range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still worried I’ll end up back here again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That’s why we’re setting up visiting nurses to help you at home with insulin and blood sugar checks twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s helpful. What about my mental health? I’ve been feeling really down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry recommended continuing your sertraline and adding outpatient therapy. They also suggested psychiatric visiting nurses to check in weekly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t like the last crisis center. It felt scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You won’t be going back there. This is about support at home—helping you stay on track with both your physical and mental health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your blood work this morning is excellent. Glucose is 90, no ketones, and your electrolytes are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you keep doing this well. We’ll finalize your discharge plan today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue 28 units of Lantus at night, Humalog with meals, and the new H. pylori treatment for 14 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The antibiotics and Protonix?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—amoxicillin, levofloxacin, and pantoprazole. It’s important to finish all of them, even if you feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tramadol every 4 hours as needed, acetaminophen every 8 hours, and the lidocaine patch daily. And please follow up with physical therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve arranged for home health to visit twice daily for insulin education and blood sugar monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I sometimes get confused with the sliding scale.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They’ll help you feel more confident. Also, GI wants to see you in two weeks to check on your stomach treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my primary doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, follow up with them in one week. They’ll coordinate your diabetes, back pain, and mental health care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. You’ve done really well—your labs are normal, and you’re eating and moving well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m nervous, but I’ll try to stick to the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to support you. Call your doctor if your blood sugar goes above 300 or below 70, or if you start vomiting again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my back pain gets worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Try the tramadol and acetaminophen first. If it doesn’t help, or if you have numbness or weakness, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I still check my blood sugar four times a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with the sliding scale insulin. The visiting nurses will help you review the logs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And no alcohol with the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly—avoid alcohol while on levofloxacin and for a few days after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing all the right things. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. The discharge nurse will go over your meds and paperwork now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi… I’ve been really nauseous since this morning. Started vomiting after I took my pills. And my back pain came back bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did you take your medications on an empty stomach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I took them first thing, then laid down about 15 minutes later. That’s when the nausea hit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That might be part of the problem. Lying down after taking pills can irritate your stomach. We’ll give you something for nausea and start IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I just hate being here again. I was only home a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You’ve been through a lot lately. Let’s focus on getting you feeling better today. We’ll check your blood sugar and run some tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar is 132, which is good — no ketoacidosis this time. Your labs are mostly normal. No signs of infection or pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my diabetes acting up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not this time. But your nausea could be related to your gastroparesis — that’s delayed stomach emptying from diabetes. We’re continuing your metoclopramide to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics? I’m still on those for H. pylori?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping you on amoxicillin, levofloxacin, and pantoprazole for your stomach inflammation. That should help reduce irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My back pain got worse when I was vomiting. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, retching can strain your back muscles. Your pain is consistent with your chronic back pain from the old car accident. No red flags.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No MRI this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. The pain team last time recommended continuing acetaminophen and tramadol. We’ll keep that up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an abdominal X-ray to check for a blockage. Good news — no obstruction or ileus. Your bowel looks normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not something serious like a blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. It’s likely your chronic stomach issues flaring up, possibly from how you took your meds this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to stop ending up here so often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re working on that. Social work met with your family. You’ll have visiting nurses at home and help with transportation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That might help. I’ve been missing my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I haven’t thrown up since yesterday. Nausea’s much less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your heart rate has also come down — it was high yesterday from dehydration and pain, but fluids helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was really anxious in the ER. They gave me Ativan but it didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We’re being careful with sedatives since you’re allergic to prochlorperazine. But we can talk about managing anxiety better as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just get so overwhelmed with everything — diabetes, pain, meds. It’s a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It absolutely is. That’s why we’re setting up home support. And we’re adding a new medication — Zofran ODT, a dissolving tablet for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help more than what I’m on now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might give you faster relief. Take it under the tongue when nausea starts. But still take your regular meds with food and stay upright.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well overnight. You’re tolerating liquids, and your pain is controlled. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s good. What about my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on your usual regimen — Lantus at night and sliding scale lispro. Your sugars have been stable, so no changes needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics? I was supposed to be on them for 14 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll finish the course at home. We’re adjusting the pantoprazole to twice daily and shortening the antibiotic duration since you’re improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’re finalizing your discharge. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just… what do I do if the nausea comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take the Zofran ODT as needed. Stay upright after meds, eat small meals, and call your doctor if it doesn’t improve. And keep up with your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thank you… for listening. I feel a bit more hopeful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re here to help. You’ll be going home with nursing visits and community support. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been feeling nauseous and vomiting since this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, right after I took my pills on an empty stomach. I couldn’t keep anything down all day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You went to the ER earlier and got fluids, Zofran, and Dilaudid. But the nausea didn’t improve much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. I still felt sick. The Zofran ODT didn’t help at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any belly pain, diarrhea, or constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No stomach pain. Just my usual back pain. But I’ve been nauseous all day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Your labs came back — no infection, no kidney issues, and your glucose was 87 when you arrived. That’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not DKA or anything serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not this time. Your anion gap is normal, so we’re not worried about ketoacidosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But why does this keep happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, it’s likely related to your gastroparesis — delayed stomach emptying from diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my stomach just doesn’t move food along?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And taking meds on an empty stomach can trigger nausea. We’ll keep you on bowel rest tonight — no food, just IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Will I be able to eat tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small sips in the morning. If you tolerate that, we’ll try light food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? I’m worried about my sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring your fingersticks. Since you’re not eating, we lowered your Lantus to 24 units tonight to avoid low sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually take 28 at night. Is it safe to go lower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, temporarily. Once you’re eating normally again, you’ll go back to 28.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still getting your amoxicillin, levofloxacin, and pantoprazole for your H. pylori treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And Reglan? That usually helps with nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding the oral Reglan for now since you can’t keep pills down. But we’ll restart it when you can eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about pain? My back’s been bothering me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can have tramadol as needed. We’ll avoid morphine — you’re allergic, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and Prochlorperazine too. Tramadol is fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I haven’t vomited since last night. Can I try some water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with ice chips and clear liquids. If that stays down, we’ll advance to a light meal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. And my blood sugar was low this morning — 46.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that was during the night. It confirms we did the right thing lowering your Lantus. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I should keep it at 24 until I’m eating normally?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Once you’re back on regular meals, go back to 28 units at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with the clear liquids. Ready to try a soft meal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m hungry. Maybe some toast and applesauce?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll bring that shortly. And we’re restarting Reglan with meals to help with stomach emptying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been doing really well — tolerating food, no nausea, no vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Can I go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discharging you. Just a few things to go over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, what do I need to know?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your meds, including the antibiotics for H. pylori. Take Reglan with meals, not four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep Lantus at 24 units tonight. When your appetite is back to normal, increase it to 28.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Any follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, see your primary doctor in a few weeks. Call if nausea returns or you can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel a low sugar coming on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Treat it with fast-acting sugar — juice or glucose tabs. And check your levels four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have my meter with me. I’ll keep up with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. You’re cleared to go home. Take it easy, eat small meals, and don’t take pills on an empty stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — my back pain is better, but should I restart my tramadol at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as needed. Just don’t exceed one every four hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And Zofran — same as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one every six hours as needed for nausea. But call if you need it more than twice in a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I’ll play it safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again for helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your doctors here. You were admitted for nausea and vomiting, especially in the mornings. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been going on for a few days now. I wake up and just start vomiting, even if I haven’t eaten. It feels just like my past episodes with gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned before that you saw blood in your vomit. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just a little, pink-tinged. I was worried it might be serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s called hematemesis, and it can happen from irritation in the esophagus. We’re keeping an eye on it. For now, you’re not able to keep anything down, so we’re giving you fluids through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m on NPO, right? When can I start drinking again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small sips once the nausea settles. We’ve given you Zofran through the IV, which should help. We also did a chest X-ray and an abdominal X-ray earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what did they show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — no pneumonia, no blockage in your bowels, and no free air, which means no perforation. Your labs are mostly stable too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But why am I still vomiting? Is it my diabetes again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar was 161 when you came in — not in DKA. We’re continuing your Lantus and sliding scale insulin. But since you’ve had this before, we’re thinking it could be related to your esophagus or stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Reglan before for gastroparesis, but my GI doctor stopped it recently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see that. And actually, past studies haven’t confirmed gastroparesis. So we’re considering other causes. Because of the blood in your vomit, we’re concerned about a small tear or irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Could that be serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely a small Mallory-Weiss tear from vomiting. Your hemoglobin is stable, so no active bleeding. But to be sure, GI wants to do an EGD — that’s an upper endoscopy — tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: An EGD? I’ve had one before. Is it necessary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because of the blood. It will let us see if there’s inflammation, ulcers, or varices — which are swollen veins in the esophagus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Varices? I don’t have liver disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: True, but sometimes they can occur for other reasons. We’ll take a look and maybe a biopsy if needed. You’ll be sedated, so it won’t be uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I agree. And what about my back pain? It’s been worse with all this vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know you’re on Tramadol at home. Since you can’t take pills right now, we’re giving Dilaudid through your IV, diluted and slowly infused. Once you can eat, we’ll switch back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And my anxiety — I’ve been really stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still getting your Zoloft daily, and you can take Ativan as needed. We’ve also had social work check in with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did well overnight — no vomiting. We’re going to do your EGD in a couple of hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Any updates on my blood pressure? It’s been high lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your BP has been elevated even after the vomiting stopped — around 130s/90s. We’re starting to think it’s not just from nausea. We may need to start a blood pressure med.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d rather not take another pill, but if I need to, okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from your EGD. It went well. They found mild varices in your esophagus and some patchy areas in the stomach, but no active bleeding or ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Varices? Does that mean I have liver problems?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. They’re mild, and we don’t know the cause yet. Since you don’t have liver disease, we’ll need to follow up outpatient to check why they’re there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood in my vomit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely from the varices or a small tear from vomiting. No active bleeding now. We’ve held your aspirin for now, just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take that for my heart. Should I be worried about stopping it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s precautionary. You’ll discuss restarting it with your primary doctor after your varices are evaluated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Can I start drinking now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with ice chips and clear liquids. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance your diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You kept down apple juice and broth last night — great job. We’re moving you to full liquids today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My nausea is much better. What about my insulin? I noticed my sugars were high yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on your Lantus at night and sliding scale. But we noticed you had some sweets brought in — juice, pudding. That can spike your sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess I got hungry. But I didn’t think it was a big deal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It adds up. We had a dietitian talk to you yesterday about balanced choices, especially with diabetes and kidney concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she was helpful. I’ll try to do better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Also, we started you on Lisinopril yesterday for your blood pressure. We’ll keep you on it and monitor your potassium and kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll take that at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 10 mg daily. We’ll check your labs at your follow-up to make sure it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well — no nausea, no pain, and you’re tolerating full liquids. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to follow up with your primary doctor this week. They’ll check your blood work because of the new blood pressure medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the varices?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll need a GI follow-up to evaluate them further. And discuss with your doctor when it’s safe to restart aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I can go back to my regular insulin and Tramadol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home meds except aspirin. Take Prilosec daily, Zofran as needed for nausea, and Ativan for anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs look good, and you’ve had no issues overnight. We’re clearing you to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Just remember: call your doctor this week, get your labs done, and follow up with GI about the varices.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And if I start vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your Zofran. If it doesn’t help or you see blood, come back to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my blood pressure — should I monitor it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you can, that would help your doctor. Otherwise, they’ll check it at your visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I have a monitor at home. I’ll start using it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we’ll see you around only if you need us — but hopefully not!

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been feeling really nauseous and vomiting all day. I couldn’t even keep my morning meds down—well, I did take my insulin, but nothing else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Was the vomit bloody or green at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, it wasn’t bloody or green. Just clear and stomach contents. I haven’t had any pain, but I just can’t eat or drink without throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I see you were just discharged a few days ago with similar symptoms. This seems to be part of a pattern. We’ll give you some IV fluids and anti-nausea medication to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it keeps happening. And I’ve been so tired and emotional lately. It’s hard to cope.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’ll make sure you’re supported. I also see you mentioned frequent urination—any burning or urgency?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No burning, but I’ve been going a lot more than usual. That’s why I went to the ER earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. Your urine test showed signs of infection, so we gave you an antibiotic in the ER. We’ll monitor that. For now, we’ll keep you on IV fluids and give you Zofran for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. Will I be able to eat soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small sips once the nausea settles. Your potassium was low, so we’re replacing that too. We want to make sure you can keep things down before advancing your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling? Any nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, actually. I haven’t vomited since last night. I sipped some water and it stayed down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’re going to try advancing your diet to clear liquids. Also, we got your urine culture back—it shows a common skin bacteria, likely contamination, so we’ll stop the ciprofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So I don’t need that antibiotic anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for the urine. But we’re starting a new antibiotic regimen for something else. Remember the endoscopy you had recently? It showed H. pylori, a stomach bacteria that can cause nausea and gastritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I remember. They said I had gastritis. But I never got treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. So we’re starting you on amoxicillin and levofloxacin for two weeks to treat the H. pylori. You’ll also take omeprazole twice daily to help your stomach heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help with the vomiting long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should. H. pylori can worsen gastroparesis, which we think you have due to your diabetes. Treating the infection may reduce your nausea episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. What about my blood pressure? It’s been high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing your lisinopril. You were on 10 mg, but we increased it to 20 mg daily since your blood pressure was still elevated. We’ll monitor your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been forgetting to take it sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But it’s important for your kidneys and heart, especially with diabetes. We’ll go over your meds before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound of your upper abdomen today to check your liver, since your last endoscopy showed possible varices.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. The varices. Does that mean I have liver disease?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. The ultrasound was normal—liver looks healthy, no blockages. But we’re still checking for hepatitis and other causes. Those results are pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it might not be serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s too early to say, but the normal ultrasound is reassuring. You’ll follow up with GI to monitor the varices and review the blood tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your mood been? I noticed you’ve been tearful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Honestly, not great. I’ve been feeling down for months. It’s hard managing everything—diabetes, pain, being in and out of the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. We’ve involved social work to help with support and coping. We’re also continuing your sertraline and will make sure you have a follow-up with your mental health provider.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I really appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’ve had no nausea overnight, labs are improving, and you tolerated a regular diet last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re going to discharge you today. You’ll go home on the amoxicillin and levofloxacin for two weeks, plus omeprazole twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin and lisinopril?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue your Lantus and Novolog as before. Lisinopril 10 mg daily—back to your original dose. And keep taking sertraline for your mood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When should I follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your primary doctor in a week. GI in two weeks to review your H. pylori treatment and varices. And keep working with your counselor. You’re doing well—keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have the nurse go over your discharge instructions and prescriptions. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. You’re here because of nausea, vomiting, and feeling shaky. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been vomiting clear stuff for two days, couldn’t keep anything down. I was up all night with back pain and nausea. This morning I felt trembly and shaky after taking my Zoloft.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were on sertraline, tramadol, and Zofran. There’s a concern that these together might have caused a reaction called serotonin syndrome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Serotonin syndrome? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but yours seems mild. Toxicology reviewed your case and didn’t think it was full-blown. Still, we’ll stop tramadol and Zofran to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I need something for nausea. I’ve had gastroparesis for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use Reglan instead of Zofran. It’s safer for you. And we’re giving IV fluids because you’re dehydrated from vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My heart’s been racing too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your heart rate was in the 120s. That could be from dehydration or the serotonin concern. We’re monitoring you on telemetry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also have bad back pain from an old car accident. I’ve been taking Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. But long-term opioids aren’t recommended for you. We’re switching to a lidocaine patch, Tylenol, and tizanidine at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that be enough? The pain keeps me up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so. Tizanidine helps with muscle spasms and can aid sleep. But avoid driving when you take it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. What about my diabetes? I couldn’t take my insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been giving insulin through your IV. Your sugars are stabilizing. No ketones in blood, but we saw some in urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My A1C was 10.9 last time. I know it’s high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll help you manage that. You’ll go back to your home insulin regimen when you can eat again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been on antibiotics for H. pylori. I missed a few doses before coming in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing amoxicillin and levofloxacin. You’ll finish the course after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had that before and it helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray. It’s clear—no pneumonia or fluid. Your ultrasound was also normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the urine test? I saw bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had some bacteria and white cells, but no symptoms of infection. It’s called asymptomatic bacteriuria—no treatment needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my mood’s been low. I was on Zoloft, but now it’s stopped?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We paused sertraline because of the possible reaction. Psychiatry thinks you may benefit from restarting it later, without tramadol or Zofran.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel better with it, but the nausea made me stop before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll coordinate with your PCP and psychiatrist. It’s important you follow up after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving. Heart rate is down to 95, and you’re less shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a bit better. Can I try eating something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with clear liquids. If that goes well, we’ll advance your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m so tired of being NPO.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated apple juice and broth. We’re moving you to a soft diet—mashed potatoes, applesauce.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My back feels a little better with the new meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep monitoring. Your insulin doses are adjusting with your meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning look great. Anion gap is normal, no ketones. Heart rate is 88.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t vomited since yesterday morning. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow. We want to make sure you can keep food down and your sugars stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my meds when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue amoxicillin and levofloxacin for four more days, omeprazole daily. Stop tramadol and Zofran for good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Zoloft?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your PCP will decide if and when to restart it. But never with tramadol or Zofran.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have appointments with your PCP, a pain specialist, and social work. They’ll help coordinate care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve missed some before. I’ll try this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s very important. You’ve had multiple admissions. A team approach can help prevent that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re discharging you today. You’re eating, sugars are stable, and symptoms resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember: no tramadol or Zofran. Use the lidocaine patch, tizanidine, and Tylenol for pain. Take your antibiotics as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll call to reschedule if I can’t make a follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your health depends on these appointments. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. A nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your urine culture was negative, so no infection. And your anemia is mild, likely from chronic disease. Monitor it with your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll keep that in mind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your blood pressure was a bit high. Keep taking lisinopril daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I sometimes forget, but I’ll try to be more consistent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That would help. We’re all here to support you. Just keep in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. The nurse will finalize everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If symptoms return—vomiting, shaking, high sugars—come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to be back here soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t either. That’s why follow-up is key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi… I’ve been so nauseous all day. I’ve thrown up a few times and my chest feels tight. It just got too much, so I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any pain when you breathe or signs of blood in your vomit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood, no diarrhea either. Just this awful nausea and the tightness in my chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. We checked your heart and lungs — your ECG was normal and your chest X-ray looks clear. No signs of infection or blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart? That’s a relief… but why am I so sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar was high — 259 — which can slow down your stomach. That’s called gastroparesis, and it causes nausea. But we also think your anxiety is playing a big role.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Anxiety? I’ve been stressed, yes… but I feel like my body is failing me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Your history shows you’ve had panic attacks before. When they flare up, they can cause real physical symptoms — nausea, chest tightness, even vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s in my head? That’s what people always say…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s not 'just in your head.' Your body is reacting to stress. It’s real, and it’s treatable. We’ve started you on IV fluids and gave you Reglan for the nausea and Ativan for anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did feel a little better after the Ativan… but I’m scared this will keep happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Your diabetes needs better control — your A1C is 10.9, which is quite high. That’s contributing to the stomach issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know… I’ve been struggling to keep up with my insulin. Life’s been overwhelming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. We’re not here to judge. We want to support you. Psychiatry also saw you and thinks exposure therapy could help with your anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They mentioned that… I’m open to it, but I’ve missed a lot of appointments before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work with social work to help coordinate your follow-ups. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous, but less anxious. Can I eat something? I’m so hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on clear liquids tonight. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance your diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my back pain? It’s flaring up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. We’re continuing your lidocaine patch, Tylenol, and tizanidine. We’re avoiding opioids because of past reactions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand… but it’s hard to cope when the pain is this bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hear you. Pain management is important. We’ll keep monitoring and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through the night without vomiting. That’s progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had some apple juice and crackers. I think I can handle more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll upgrade you to a soft diet. And your blood pressure came down — that’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember you tried clonidine yesterday. Did that help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It helped a little with both anxiety and blood pressure, but you had one low reading, so we stopped it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to pass out… but I do need help calming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The Ativan is still available as needed. And we’re keeping your insulin on track to help your stomach empty better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I’m worried… I haven’t been to my GI or psych appointments. I feel like I keep failing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not failing. You’re here, and that’s what matters. You said you finished your H. pylori antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, this time I did. But do I need another scope?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to confirm it’s gone. Also, you have Grade I esophageal varices, so another EGD is needed to check those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That scares me… but I’ll do it if it’s necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is. But we’ll help you schedule it. Social work is setting up a care team to support you after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. No vomiting, you’re eating, and your mood is better. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s good… but I’m nervous about going back to the same routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But you’ll go home with the same meds: insulin, lisinopril, Ativan as needed, and your pain patch. And we’ll set up close follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will someone help me keep track of everything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Social work will call you, and we’ll coordinate with your PCP, GI, and psychiatry. You’re not alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you… I really want to get better this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we believe you can. Keep using your Ativan when your heart races or nausea starts — it’s okay to use it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin — I’ll keep taking 28 units at night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and use your sliding scale during the day. Check your sugars regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. I promise I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. We’ll see you in follow-up soon. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. Any nausea or chest tightness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel much better. Still anxious, but not panicking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Remember — your symptoms are linked to both blood sugar and anxiety. Managing both is key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep that in mind. Thank you for not giving up on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t give up on our patients. You’re strong — keep going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I’m ready. I’ll call social work when I get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please do. And if nausea returns or your sugars are high, don’t wait — call your doctor or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned my body can’t handle being ignored anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a powerful realization. Use it. We’re here for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. Really.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I woke up with bad back pain. I tried heating pads, but then I started feeling nauseous and threw up twice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did you notice anything else—like fever, chest pain, or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. But my blood sugar was 215 when I checked it. Then my anxiety started kicking in, so I called the ambulance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. In the ER, your blood sugar was actually much higher—623. We’ve given you fluids and your home insulin to bring it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh wow, that’s really high. I didn’t feel that bad, but I guess the nausea distracted me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, nausea and anxiety can mask how high your sugars are. We also saw your sodium was low—126—which can happen with high glucose and dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if it drops too low, but we’re correcting it slowly with IV fluids. You’re already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My back still hurts, though. I was supposed to get a lidocaine patch, but it wasn’t approved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see that. You’ve had back pain since your car accident, right? We can give you acetaminophen and tizanidine tonight. If it flares, we may use a short-acting pain med.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that would help. I just hate being in pain—it makes my anxiety worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ve given you a dose of lorazepam to help with the nausea and anxiety. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The nausea’s gone, and I feel calmer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll keep monitoring your blood sugar. It was 206 a few hours ago—much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I checked your labs this morning—your sodium is now 137, and creatinine improved from 1.2 to 0.9. That means your kidneys are responding well to fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My back feels okay this morning. No nausea at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to advance your diet to clear liquids and see how you tolerate it. If all goes well, you can have regular food later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have juice? I’m worried about low sugar now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check your blood sugar before each meal. If it’s low, we’ll give you juice or glucose tabs. For now, let’s start with broth and crackers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You kept down lunch, and your blood sugar was 180 before it. We’re going to keep your Lantus insulin at 32 units tonight to see how it works.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait, I usually take 28. Is 32 safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We increased it because your sugars were high. But if you go low in the morning, we’ll adjust it down. Safety first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve had lows before—they scare me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. We’ll monitor closely. Your Novolog sliding scale will help fine-tune things around meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We had a small issue—your blood sugar dropped to 68 this morning. That’s why we’re lowering your Lantus back to 30 units tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t even feel that. Was I awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were, and you had juice. But it shows we need to be careful with insulin increases. 30 units should be safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I just want to avoid highs and lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re balancing that. Your kidney function is stable, so we’ll keep your lisinopril for blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your nausea came back once this morning, but you tolerated a full lunch right after. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it was just a quick wave. I’m feeling fine now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your back pain flared a bit, so we gave you one dose of oxycodone. It’s resolved now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s much better. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you today. You’re tolerating food, your sugars are more stable, and your labs have improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your lisinopril, take tizanidine at night for muscle relaxation, and use lorazepam as needed for anxiety. We’re increasing your Lantus to 30 units at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Novolog?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using it with meals as before. We’re also giving you Zofran for nausea, just in case, for the next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I see any specialists?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We strongly recommend seeing an endocrinologist for your diabetes and a pain specialist for your back. Also, mental health support is key—your anxiety often triggers these episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I’ve been avoiding it, but I see now it’s important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve arranged for you to switch your primary care to a new provider at our clinic. You’ll need to call to confirm the change before your appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have a nurse go over your discharge instructions and medications before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my lidocaine patch still isn’t approved. Can we fix that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ve sent a request to pain management. They’ll review it. In the meantime, keep using acetaminophen and tizanidine as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow up with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Your discharge order is in. You’re doing well—eating normally, no nausea, back pain controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and please follow up with your new providers. Call us if your nausea returns or your blood sugar goes too high or low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. You’re here because of nausea and vomiting again, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been vomiting all day. I tried the Zofran I have at home, but it didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your blood sugars—how have they been?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They’ve been in the 150s to 200s. I took my Lantus last night at 10, like usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. No signs of diabetic ketoacidosis, which is reassuring. Did you eat anything this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried some toast and soda, but I threw it all up. Then my back pain got worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any abdominal pain, diarrhea, or other symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no belly pain or anything like that. Just the nausea, vomiting, and now my back is really bothering me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. In the ER, you got some IV Zofran, ketorolac, and Dilaudid. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. The nausea is calmer, but my back still aches.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep managing that. Your labs look stable—no infection, kidneys are okay, and your electrolytes are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I was worried about my sugars or kidneys again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching closely. Since you have type 1 diabetes, we want to avoid both high and low sugars. You had one mild low this morning, but you treated it with food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, around 6 AM. I had some juice and it came back up. But I ate a cracker after that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good job catching that. We’ll keep your insulin the same as before—no changes to your Lantus or Novolog.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I don’t want to go too low again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Now, about the nausea—since Zofran ODT isn’t helping at home, we’re suggesting you try Ativan next time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ativan? Like for anxiety? But I’m not anxious when I’m nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can help with nausea too, especially in people with diabetes. It works on the brain’s nausea center. And since you already take lorazepam, it’s safe to try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So instead of Zofran, take Ativan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 1 mg. We’re updating your prescription so you can try it next time symptoms start.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll give it a shot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’ve been doing well—no vomiting since this morning, and you sipped some broth without issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel much better. Still a little queasy, but not throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to advance your diet to a regular diabetic meal tomorrow. If you keep this up, you could go home tomorrow afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What about my back pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on gabapentin—200 mg three times a day. It’s for nerve-related pain and might help more than tizanidine did.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t keep taking tizanidine—it didn’t help. But I liked the lidocaine patch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But insurance requires a trial of gabapentin first. If this doesn’t work, we can apply for the patches.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So I have to try this first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And you can increase the dose slowly—by 200 mg each week, up to 400 mg three times a day, if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So start at 200, then go up if it’s not helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. But don’t go over 1200 mg a day unless we say so.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I can still use the menthol cream and acetaminophen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both are fine. Use them as needed for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did great overnight—no vomiting, ate breakfast without issues, and your sugars are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discharging you today. Keep taking the gabapentin daily, even if your back feels okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if it doesn’t help, I can call about the lidocaine patches?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Also, try Ativan next time nausea starts. And keep following up with your new care team, especially the Chronic Pain Service.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you only if you really need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in this morning for nausea, vomiting, and high blood sugar. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I ate potato salad and meat last night, and by bedtime I felt nauseous. I had two loose stools. This morning I threw up and my blood sugar was 600 in the ambulance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had this before. Were you able to keep anything down after vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. I took Zofran but it didn’t help much. I got scared and called the ambulance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was the right call. Your blood sugar was very high—627 when you arrived—but you’re not in diabetic ketoacidosis, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not DKA? I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, your labs show no acidosis. We gave you IV insulin to bring it down. We also gave Zofran and Dilaudid for nausea and discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My stomach still feels off, but the pain is better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your exam shows no serious abdominal issues. Lungs are clear, heart normal. We did a chest X-ray to check for infection—it’s fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having a lot of back pain too, since my car accident years ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see you’re on gabapentin and Tylenol. We’ll continue those. No point tenderness in your back, so no new injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes… it’s always so hard to control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll talk more about that. For now, we’re starting you on fluids and will try to get you on a regular diet later today if you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’ve been doing well—no vomiting, and you kept down some crackers. We’re going to advance you to a regular diabetic diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I was worried I’d throw it up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor closely. Your blood sugar was high earlier after ice chips—did you know they have sugar in them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I didn’t! I thought it was just water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a common mistake. We’ll go over diet counseling to help avoid surprises like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood work came back. Your kidney function was a bit off when you arrived—creatinine 1.2—but it’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from my diabetes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it suggests early diabetic nephropathy. But staying hydrated and controlling your sugar helps protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know my kidneys were involved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s stage I, so very early. But it’s another reason to focus on tight glucose control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been trying… but my sugars swing so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed. You had a low sugar this morning—down to 60—after treating a high with too much insulin overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just wanted it to come down fast… I get so anxious when it’s high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That’s actually something we want to talk about—your anxiety and how it affects your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes the nausea feels like it’s from panic, not my stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry saw you and thinks some episodes may be linked to anxiety ‘flooding,’ but this time, your symptoms may have been from food or high sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not all of it is in my head?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. We did a gastric emptying study yesterday—it was normal. So it’s not gastroparesis this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that test before and it was normal too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. So we’re focusing on diabetes control and possible gastroenteritis from the potato salad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back—no infection. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I didn’t have a blood infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Your symptoms weren’t from sepsis. We’re confident it’s related to your diabetes and possibly the food you ate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your A1C result—it’s 12.8%. That means your average sugar has been very high, around 321 mg/dL.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s worse than I thought.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We consulted diabetes management. They recommend keeping your Lantus at 28 units at night, but adjusting how you count carbs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought I was doing it right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You are trying, but we’re changing your ratio to 1 unit of Humalog for every 12 grams of carbs—was it 1:10 before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think so. And the sliding scale?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take 1 unit of Humalog for every 40 points your sugar is above 140. We’ll give you a chart to follow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s different. I’ll need to write it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and keep a log of your finger sticks. It’ll help your new doctor see patterns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve set up a lot for you before discharge tomorrow. You’ll see a new primary care provider in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve missed a lot of appointments before… I feel bad about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. That’s why a social worker will go with you to your first visit. They’ll help you connect with a therapist too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That would really help. I want to do better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. You also have a GI follow-up to repeat an endoscopy for your stomach varices and check if H. pylori is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well—no nausea, eating normally, sugars stable. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
