conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue Lantus 28 units at night, Humalog with meals using the new ratio. Gabapentin is now 200 mg three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was 200 mg every 8 hours before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same total dose—just adjusted for easier timing. We’re also adding Zofran as a backup for nausea, but try Ativan first if anxiety is involved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pharmacy has your insulin and supplies. Keep checking your sugars and write them down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll go to the appointments—I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to support you. Call if your sugar is very high or low, or if vomiting returns. Otherwise, we’ll see how you do at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and good luck with your new care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi… I’ve been feeling really sick. Nauseous, throwing up, and my back pain’s been worse. My blood sugar’s been really high too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. When did the high blood sugars start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Two days ago. I wasn’t eating much because I felt off, but I kept taking my Lantus at night like usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And when did the vomiting start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yesterday. I couldn’t keep anything down, so I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your blood sugar was 595 when you arrived, and we saw some ketones. That means you were in diabetic ketoacidosis. We gave you insulin and fluids in the ER to start correcting it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I didn’t realize it was that bad. I thought it was just another high sugar episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was serious, but we’ve already started treatment. Your anion gap is closing, which means the acidosis is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good… I hate feeling this way. It happens a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know this isn’t the first time. We’re going to keep you NPO for now—no food or drink by mouth—for the next few hours to let your stomach settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I get something for the nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve given you Reglan and ondansetron through your IV. You should start feeling better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. What about my back pain? It’s been really bothering me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your back—no tenderness. It might be related to your high sugars or muscle tension. We gave you dilaudid earlier, and we can continue with pain meds as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. I’ve had back pain since my car accident years ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see that in your history. You’re on gabapentin—still helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it helps some. I also use the lidocaine patch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep that up. We also did a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis to make sure there’s nothing else going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was there anything wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scan was clear—no abscess, no blockage. Your liver and pancreas look normal too. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried it might be my stomach again—like the gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know you’ve had that diagnosis, but your recent gastric emptying study was normal. Still, high sugars can make nausea worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I just don’t always know what triggers the highs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work with the endocrinology team to adjust your insulin. They recommend lowering your Lantus dose to 24 units at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: From 28? Why is that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because we want to avoid lows, especially since you’re not eating. We’ll also give you a tighter sliding scale for your Humalog.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can follow that. I’ve messed up before by overcorrecting at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that in your last admission. It’s important to balance correction without going too low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugar last night dropped to 230 and stayed in the 200s. This morning it’s 179—much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I eat something now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re going to start you on clear liquids and slowly advance to a regular diet. We’ll watch how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m really hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with the clear liquids. We’re upgrading you to a regular diet for lunch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. No nausea so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your kidney function was a little off on admission—creatinine was 1.5—but it’s improving with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from dehydration?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and possibly from your lisinopril. We held it temporarily, but we’ll restart it today since your levels are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I know I need to drink more water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. Your blood sugars are stable—no highs or lows—and you’ve kept your meals down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discharging you today. We’ve updated your insulin: 24 units of glargine at bedtime and a new sliding scale for your aspart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need to review the sheet carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ve also set up follow-up with your PCP, a counselor through social work, and GI for your esophageal varices.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve missed some appointments before… but I want to do better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great step. Your team is here to support you. Keep using your nausea med as needed, and monitor your sugars closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me through this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call your doctor if you start feeling unwell again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were admitted last night after coming to the ER with nausea, vomiting, and some back pain. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not great. I’ve been sick all night. I drank orange juice after I got home yesterday and it made me vomit right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That sounds like your gastroparesis acting up again. We’re keeping you on bowel rest for now—no food or drink by mouth—so your stomach can settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m so hungry. How long will I have to go without eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start small once the vomiting stops. For now, we’re giving you fluids and medications through your IV to keep you hydrated and control nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My back hurts too. Can I get something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re managing your pain with IV medications. But we’re being careful because some painkillers can worsen nausea or constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just feel so overwhelmed. I’m tired of being sick all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. It’s a lot to manage. We’ve asked Psychiatry to see you to help talk through some of this. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your blood sugar was 146 when you arrived—good, no ketoacidosis. But your creatinine is up to 1.6, which means your kidneys aren’t filtering well right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? My kidneys were bad before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s acute kidney injury, likely from dehydration. We’re giving you IV fluids to help. It should improve as you stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also found a urinary tract infection. Your urine test showed bacteria, and the culture grew coagulase-negative staph.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t even feel like I had a UTI. Shouldn’t I have burning or something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not always. With diabetes, infections can be silent. We’re treating it with antibiotics—started on Cipro, now switching to Macrobid to finish the course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had some diarrhea too. We think this could be gastroenteritis on top of your gastroparesis flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not just my diabetes acting up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s both. The infection and vomiting are making it harder for your stomach to empty, which is why we’re keeping you NPO for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been high—149/100 earlier. We gave IV metoprolol since you’re not eating. Once you can take pills, we’ll restart lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot to take it before I came in. I’ve been so stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. We’ll get it back on track. We’re planning to increase it to 20 mg daily to help control your BP better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your IV stopped working last night, so we’re going to place a PICC line today to make giving fluids and meds easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s a PICC line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a longer IV line that goes into a vein in your arm and up toward your heart. It’ll stay in for a few days to avoid needing new IVs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line was placed successfully this morning. You’re now getting fluids and antibiotics through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels weird in my arm. Is it supposed to go all the way to my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it goes into a large vein near your heart. A chest X-ray confirmed it’s in the right spot. You might see it on the monitor—it extends a bit into the right atrium, but that’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is coming down—from 1.6 to 1.2. That’s a good sign your kidneys are recovering with hydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I try drinking something now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small sips of water. If you keep that down, we’ll advance to clear liquids tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well last night—no vomiting. We’re going to start you on a diabetic liquid diet and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have insulin with it? I don’t want my sugar to spike.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re back on your full dose of Lantus—24 units at bedtime—and we’ll use Humalog as a sliding scale with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry met with you yesterday. They think your anxiety is playing a big role in how you’re coping with your health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just feel out of control. When I get anxious, I can’t move, I can’t think.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. Social work is helping find a new counselor for you. They also suggest restarting an SSRI to help manage the anxiety long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve kept down the liquid diet. We’re going to advance you to soft foods—mashed potatoes, applesauce—still diabetic-friendly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have Reglan with meals? It usually helps my stomach empty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve restarted Reglan—now four times a day instead of three. That should help with gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you’ve had no nausea or vomiting for two days. Your blood pressure is also much better on the increased lisinopril dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. We’ll make sure you can keep down solid food and that your blood sugars are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We had a family meeting with social work. We talked about how stress and anxiety might be making your physical symptoms worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t say much, but I heard you. I do want to feel better—mentally too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great step. We’ll get you set up with follow-up for both your PCP and a counselor. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. You’re eating regular food, no vomiting, and your labs are improving. We’re planning to discharge you this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my meds? Anything changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Lisinopril is now 20 mg daily, Reglan is four times a day, and you’ll continue Zofran as needed. Insulin stays the same—24 units Lantus at night and Humalog with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the Macrobid as prescribed. Drink plenty of fluids to prevent another UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. And I’ll call to set up that counseling appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the plan. Get your labs checked soon to make sure your kidneys and electrolytes are stable. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to go home. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it. Thank you for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself, and don’t hesitate to call if things worsen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi… I’ve been so sick. Nauseous, throwing up, and I had diarrhea all night. My blood sugar was really high too—over 500 when I checked it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were started on IV fluids and insulin in the ER. We think you’re in diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA. That happens when your body doesn’t have enough insulin and starts breaking down fat for energy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… that sounds bad. I took my Lantus last night like I always do. I don’t know why this happened.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes DKA can be triggered by stress—emotional or physical—even if you’re doing everything right with your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I’ve been going through a lot. I just told my mom last week that I was abused as a kid. It’s been really hard to talk about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m so sorry you went through that. Thank you for sharing. That kind of emotional stress can absolutely affect your body, including your blood sugar control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize it could make me this sick. I just felt overwhelmed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It makes sense. We’re treating your DKA with IV fluids and an insulin drip. Your labs show your kidneys were stressed, but they’re improving with hydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My kidneys again? I’ve had issues before with that from diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your creatinine was elevated at 1.6, but it’s coming down. That’s a sign we’re helping. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… and my nausea? It’s still there, just not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you Zofran for that. You have gastroparesis, which means your stomach empties slowly. That can make nausea worse, especially during stress or high sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Reglan for that. Should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart it once you can keep fluids down. We paused it briefly because of your vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my back pain? It’s been flaring up too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you Dilaudid earlier, but we’ll try to avoid strong opioids. They can slow your stomach even more and make gastroparesis worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I used to take gabapentin. It helped, but I stopped because it made me nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible the nausea was from your DKA or gastroparesis, not the gabapentin. We can try restarting it at a low dose and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That might be worth trying. I don’t want to rely on narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll start with 100 mg twice a day and go slow. Also, we placed a PICC line earlier today so we can give you fluids and meds safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I saw the chest X-ray. Was that to check the line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the tip was a bit too far in, but it’s in a safe spot. No issues with your lungs or heart. Everything looks clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugar is much better—down to 150. Your anion gap has closed, which means the DKA is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I eat something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with clear liquids. If you keep that down, we’ll advance your diet. Also, your urine culture grew some staph, but it’s coagulase-negative—likely not causing infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like last time? I had that before and didn’t need antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. No signs of UTI—no fever, no pain—so we won’t treat it. Blood cultures were negative, so no bloodstream infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I don’t need more meds if I don’t have to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve been tolerating a full diet, and your nausea is much better. We’re switching you from the insulin drip to regular insulin shots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I still take Lantus at night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’re reducing it from 24 to 17 units. You had a few low sugars yesterday, so we’re adjusting to keep you safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was shaky once. I didn’t want to overcorrect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Smart. We’ll keep your sliding scale for meals. Your hemoglobin is a bit low, but stable. It’s been that way for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: From my kidneys, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Chronic kidney disease can cause anemia. We’ll monitor it, but no treatment needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re looking great. Labs this morning are almost all normal. Creatinine is 0.9, glucose 95, anion gap closed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if all goes well. We’ll set up follow-up with your diabetes team and your pharmacist to review your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my gabapentin? I’ve been taking it and it’s helping my back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Keep taking it twice daily. If it stays helpful and doesn’t cause nausea, you can increase to 200 mg twice daily with your doctor’s okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my mental health? I’ve been feeling a little better talking about things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. Social work will help you connect with counseling. It’s brave to face this, and support can make a big difference.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. Your condition is stable. We’re sending you home with updated meds and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel so much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Key things: Lantus is now 17 units at night, gabapentin 100 mg twice daily, and keep using your sliding scale.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And avoid the strong painkillers unless absolutely necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They can worsen your stomach issues. Call your doctor if your sugars are too high or too low, or if you feel sick again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll follow up with social work about counseling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re strong, and you’re not alone in this. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. The nurse will go over your discharge papers and medications before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll review everything carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. And remember, emotional stress can affect your diabetes. Keep reaching out for support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m starting to learn that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big step. Take it one day at a time. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel hopeful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best thing to hear. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been vomiting and saw something dark in your vomit—can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it looked like coffee grounds. I’ve been vomiting all day. I woke up with high blood sugar and just couldn’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have type 1 diabetes and gastroparesis, right? That can definitely make nausea worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and I’ve had this before. But the coffee ground part scared me. Is there bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned about that. Your CT scan showed some changes in the esophagus, possibly from vomiting. We’ll need an endoscopy to check for any tears.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: An endoscopy? Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel it. It’s important to rule out serious bleeding. We also started you on a medication to reduce stomach acid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes me feel better. My stomach pain is gone now, at least.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We also placed a line in your groin because we couldn’t get an IV in your arm. It’s temporary and will help us give you fluids and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I noticed that. It’s a bit uncomfortable, but I understand why it’s needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on it. Your labs show your blood sugar was high earlier, but it’s coming down. We’re giving you insulin as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually take Lantus at night. Should I still take it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Since you’re not eating, we held your Lantus last night. We’ll restart it gradually. You’re getting Humalog for now based on your sugar levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I just don’t want my sugar to crash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring closely. No signs of low sugar so far. We also saw your potassium was low, so we’re giving supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Is phosphorus low too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both were low. We’re replacing them through your IV. It should correct over the next day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ve been anxious—my heart’s been racing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed your heart rate was high earlier, in the 140s. But when you rested, it came down. It seems related to anxiety, not a heart issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That happens when I’m stressed. Being in the ICU is overwhelming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll move you to the regular floor soon. It’s quieter and should help you relax.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You just had your endoscopy. The good news is no active bleeding. There’s a small erosion at the junction of your esophagus and stomach, likely from vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the coffee grounds were from that? Not a serious bleed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s called a Mallory-Weiss tear—small and usually heals on its own. We’ll keep you on a strong acid blocker to help it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I start eating soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small sips. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance slowly. Your gastroparesis means your stomach empties slowly, so we have to be cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ll be patient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving. Potassium and phosphorus are normal now. Blood sugar is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I’ve been sipping broth and haven’t vomited since yesterday afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll try a soft diet today. We also restarted your metoclopramide to help your stomach empty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that before. It helps, but sometimes makes me restless.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll watch for that. If it happens, we can adjust. Your insulin dose is back to normal—20 units Lantus tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about my diabetes being off track again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll need you to monitor sugars closely at home. Same with potassium—your levels dropped this time, so your doctor may check it in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Any restrictions when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Avoid heavy lifting for a few days because of the femoral line site. Otherwise, resume normal activities as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We removed the femoral line this morning—no issues. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What meds should I take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your usual insulin—Lantus 20 units at night, Humalog with meals. Take metoclopramide with meals, gabapentin twice daily, and Zofran if nausea returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lisinopril for blood pressure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue that daily. Follow up with your primary doctor in a week for labs and to review everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. If you vomit again or see dark stools, come back right away. Otherwise, take care and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’re here if you need us. You’re discharged now—someone will help you with the paperwork.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been really bad the last two days. I couldn’t keep anything down, and my blood sugar was all over the place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you have type 1 diabetes, correct? Were you able to take your insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried, but I was so sick. I skipped my long-acting insulin because I wasn’t eating. Now I feel shaky and confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We checked your blood work, and your glucose is very high, and there’s acid in your blood. You’re in diabetic ketoacidosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but we’re going to treat it right away with IV fluids and insulin. You’ll be closely monitored.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. My stomach hurts so much. Is that from the diabetes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be related. You also have a history of gastroparesis, which slows stomach emptying. That can cause nausea and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s been a problem for years. But this feels worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also concerned about your kidneys. Your labs show acute kidney injury, likely from dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My kidneys again? I’ve had issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your diabetes affects your kidneys. We’ll monitor your function closely and adjust your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We placed a central line in your neck last night to help with fluids and meds since your veins were hard to access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t feel that. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s standard. A chest X-ray confirmed it’s in the right spot in the upper chest vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling anxious. Is that from the illness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Being this sick can worsen anxiety and depression. We’ve noted your history and will support you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your H. pylori blood test came back positive. That’s a bacteria that can cause stomach inflammation and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can that be treated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with a two-week course of antibiotics and acid reducers. That should help your nausea and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. My back has been hurting too. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Chronic pain and backache are on your list. We’ll manage it with safe meds, avoiding those you’re allergic to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is starting to improve with fluids. Your electrolytes were off but are correcting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a bit more clear-headed today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your neuro symptoms from diabetes—like confusion—should get better as your sugars stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been coughing a little. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We heard some crackles in your lungs. Could be a mild infection. We’ll check a urine test for infection markers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I hope it’s nothing serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I need to tell you something urgent. A chest X-ray showed a large pneumothorax—collapsed lung—on the right side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What? How did that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely related to the central line placement. It’s a known risk. We call it an iatrogenic pneumothorax.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but we’re acting quickly. We’re going to insert a small tube to let the air out and let your lung re-expand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pigtail catheter was successfully placed. Another X-ray shows the lung is re-expanding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already feel like I can breathe better. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. A repeat X-ray shows no pneumothorax. The lung stayed inflated even after we pulled the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you today. Your DKA has resolved, kidney function is improving, and you’re tolerating food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my diabetes and the new H. pylori treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on your regular insulin. We’ll send prescriptions for the H. pylori antibiotics and a proton pump inhibitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my mental health? I’ve been feeling down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve documented your depression and anxiety. Please follow up with your therapist. We can refer you if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d appreciate that. And my back pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue managing it with acetaminophen. Avoid NSAIDs due to your kidney history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the varices? I remember from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your esophageal varices are still there but not bleeding. We recommend an endoscopy soon to check them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll schedule it. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll also send labs for follow-up on your blood count and electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better than when I came in. I’m glad I’m going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. Take care, and call if anything worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final chest X-ray confirms the chest tube is out and no pneumothorax returned. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I’ll follow up with my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Rest, take your meds, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel lucky to have gotten help when I did.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did the right thing coming in. Early treatment made a big difference.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll never ignore these symptoms again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best plan. Stay in touch with your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a good recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll update your primary doctor with all the details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps. I feel supported.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You should. We’re all part of your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. You’re here because of worsening abdominal pain and nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started with my usual back pain, then it moved to my stomach. I couldn’t keep anything down, not even my blood pressure pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And this happens about once a month, you said in the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, the back pain flares up, then my stomach just shuts down. It’s like a cycle. I get anxious, then the nausea gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your history of gastroparesis and anxiety probably plays into this. We’ll focus on controlling the pain and nausea so you can eat again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was in so much pain earlier, but the medicine in the ER helped a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your vitals are stable now. We’re starting IV fluids because you’ve been dehydrated from not eating. We’ll also keep an eye on your blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sugar was low in the ER, right? They gave me D50.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 70, which is low. But it’s stable now. No signs of ketoacidosis, which is good. We’ll continue your regular insulin regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve been trying to stick to my 70/30 insulin. My A1c was 9.3 last time, so I know I need to do better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s actually an improvement. We’ll keep supporting you with your diabetic diet and sliding scale insulin as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my blood pressure? I haven’t taken my lisinopril in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were hypertensive when you came in—144 over 105. We gave you one dose of lisinopril, and it helped. But we’re watching your kidney function closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My kidneys again? I’ve had issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your creatinine was 2.0 when you arrived, which is high for you. It’s come down a bit to 1.8, but not as much as we’d like.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from not drinking enough? Or is my diabetes getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely a mix—dehydration from poor intake, but also possible progression of diabetic nephropathy. We’ve stopped lisinopril for now because it can affect kidneys when they’re stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So what will I take instead?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting amlodipine, a different blood pressure medicine that’s safer for your kidneys right now. You’ll take it daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ll need to follow up with my doctor about this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ve already contacted your PCP to set up urgent follow-up with nephrology. They’ll check your kidney function and adjust meds if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I worry about my kidneys a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. We’re being proactive. Now, about your abdominal pain—your KUB scan showed no blockage or free air, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not appendicitis or something like that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. There’s an air-fluid level in your stomach, which fits with gastroparesis—your stomach isn’t emptying well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s what usually happens. Can I try eating something now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated clear liquids in the ER, so we’ll start with a light meal. We’ll go slow—small portions, easy to digest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m really hungry. I haven’t eaten in two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. We’ll get you something soon. We’re also giving ondansetron and ativan for nausea, and continuing your omeprazole for reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using ativan for anxiety and nausea. It helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll keep your usual lorazepam doses. We’re also continuing risperidone for your mood, as you’ve been seeing your psychiatrist regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Dr. ___ has been helping me a lot. The psychotic features have been better lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll keep supporting your mental health. Your ECG showed sinus tachycardia—fast heart rate—but that’s likely from pain, anxiety, and being a bit dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart’s been racing. I thought it was anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a mix. But your heart rate is coming down with fluids and symptom control. No need for extra meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You slept well, I hear. How’s your stomach today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I ate toast and applesauce last night and didn’t feel sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent progress. We’ll advance your diet to regular food today. Still some nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a little, but not bad. I used the PRN ativan last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’re minimizing narcotics to avoid constipation. You’re walking, blood pressure is better—102 over 50 now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s low, isn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s on the lower side, but you’re not dizzy or weak. Amlodipine can lower it, so we’ll monitor. Your heart rate is 107—still a bit high, but improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel calmer today. Less anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helping your body recover. We’ll plan for discharge tomorrow if you keep doing this well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’d be great. I just want to get back to my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re officially discharged today. You’ve been eating full meals, pain is controlled, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your usual meds except lisinopril—we’ve replaced it with amlodipine. Take it daily for blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow up with my PCP about my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and they’ll refer you to nephrology. Also keep seeing your psychiatrist and monitor your blood sugar closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me through this flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if the pain or nausea comes back, or if you can’t keep fluids down. Otherwise, take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You're in the hospital because you were having severe nausea and vomiting. Do you remember coming in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I felt so sick. I couldn’t stay awake. I’ve had this before with my stomach—gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. Given your history of type 1 diabetes and gastroparesis, this looks like a flare-up. You were very drowsy when you arrived, so we couldn’t talk much then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry. I just couldn’t keep my eyes open. Was my blood sugar high?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 289 when you arrived. We started you on IV fluids and adjusted your insulin because you weren’t able to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh good. I was worried I might’ve done something wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. These flares can happen even with good care. We’ve been monitoring your labs. Your kidney function is a concern—we saw your creatinine was 1.7, which is elevated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? That’s from my diabetes, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s part of diabetic kidney disease. But it’s stable for now. We’re keeping an eye on it. Your blood pressure was high too—161 over 114.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I missed a few doses of my blood pressure meds. I’ve been so nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could explain it. We restarted your lisinopril and amlodipine. Your pressure is coming down now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll try not to miss them again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I’m not vomiting anymore. Still a little nauseous, but it’s much improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’re going to try giving you small sips of water. If you keep that down, we’ll advance your diet slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope I can eat soon. I hate being on IVs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get there. Your lipase was normal, so it’s not pancreatitis. And your liver tests are okay. This is likely a gastroparesis flare, possibly triggered by stress or a mild virus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sister had a stomach bug recently, but she had diarrhea. I didn’t.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right, so it might not be the same thing. But stress and anxiety can also worsen gastroparesis. How have you been feeling mentally?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Anxious, honestly. I get panic attacks, and being sick makes it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve continued your lorazepam, mirtazapine, and risperidone. Social work also checked in with you yesterday—they said you have good support at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my sister helps me a lot. I see my therapist weekly too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve kept down clear liquids and we’ve moved you to soft foods. Your blood sugar is 178 now—much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Should I be worried about my eyes or kidneys again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your retinopathy and kidney issues are chronic, but we’re managing them. The anemia we saw—your hemoglobin is 10.2—is something to watch, likely related to kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I get tired easily. Is that from the anemia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll follow up with your PCP to check iron levels and consider treatment if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had a full meal and kept it down. That’s a big step. The endocrinology team reviewed your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on 28 units of 70/30 in the morning before. Is that changing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Temporarily, yes. While you weren’t eating, we used Lantus. Now that you’re back on meals, we’re switching you to 20 units with breakfast and 15 with dinner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll need to adjust my sliding scale too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue checking your sugars four times a day and use your sliding scale as directed. Call your doctor if they’re consistently high or low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home today. Your blood pressure is 138 over 99, and you’re alert and eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I feel so much better. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue lisinopril 20 mg and amlodipine 10 mg daily for blood pressure. Keep taking your psychiatric meds as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—20 units of 70/30 at breakfast, 15 at dinner. Make sure you eat when you take it to avoid low sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Do I need to see my specialists?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Follow up with your gastroenterologist and nephrologist. We’re also arranging an urgent endocrine appointment for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I’ll make sure to keep all my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself, and call if anything worsens—especially nausea, high sugars, or dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I worry about my back pain? It’s been acting up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be contributing to your stress and nausea. Keep managing it with your usual plan, and mention it at your next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I will. And my vision—I’ve been seeing floaters lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your diabetic retinopathy, you should see your eye doctor soon. Report any sudden vision changes immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call them this week. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. Stay hydrated, eat regularly, and keep your sugars in check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best. It’s hard sometimes, but I’m trying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re here to support you. Let’s get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Dr. Lee. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and stay in touch with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon, hopefully not in the hospital!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fingers crossed. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on my way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I was with my friend earlier today, and all of a sudden I started feeling really nauseous, then I started vomiting. I also have this dull pain in my stomach, kind of like the last time I was here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds familiar. You have gastroparesis, right? That’s when your stomach doesn’t empty properly, especially with diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. It feels just like my last flare-up. I did have a small bowel movement this morning and I’ve been passing gas, so that’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s reassuring. It means your bowels are still moving. No fever, chills, or chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none of that. Just the nausea, vomiting, and stomach ache.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. We checked your labs. Your blood sugar was 139, which is okay, and your kidney function showed a creatinine of 1.6, which is your usual baseline. But we’re watching it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My kidneys again? I know they’re not great, but I’ve been trying to stay hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have stage 3 chronic kidney disease, mostly from diabetes and high blood pressure. We’ll keep an eye on it. For now, we’re giving you IV fluids and some Zofran for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I got Zofran in the ER, but it didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see that. That’s why we’re admitting you—to give you fluids and see how you do with stronger symptom control. We’ll also keep your insulin on schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ve been using my 70/30 insulin like always, twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue that and add sliding scale if needed. Your blood pressure is a bit high at 150/90, so we’ll keep you on amlodipine and lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes it runs high when I’m stressed or sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll monitor it. For now, try to rest. A nurse will check on you regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. The nausea isn’t as bad, but I’m still not ready to eat anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. We’re going to try advancing your diet slowly. Maybe start with clear liquids later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do you think this is just another gastroparesis flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it looks like it. No signs of infection or bowel blockage. Your liver tests and lipase were normal, so it’s not pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried it might be something worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’ve been doing well. You had some apple juice and tolerated it. We’re moving you to a soft diet soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I think I might actually be hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great sign. Your stomach is starting to work again. We’ll keep the IV fluids going for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made good progress. You’ve been eating regular food and not vomiting. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still a little sore, but not bad. I only needed one dose of oxycodone yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We’ll keep it as needed. Now, I do want to talk about your kidney labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no, what’s wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine went up to 2.2. It was 1.6 when you came in. This means your kidney function dipped a bit—what we call acute on chronic kidney injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? Did I do something wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. It can happen during flares like this—sometimes from dehydration or the stress on your body. We’ve been giving you fluids, which helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So will it go back down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so. That’s why it’s important you follow up in two days for blood work with Dr. Patel at the nephrology clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll go. I know my kidneys are important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re looking great. Vital signs are stable, and your last labs show your blood sugar is well-controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. I even had toast and tea this morning with no problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’re going to discharge you today. You’ll go home with your regular meds and a small prescription for oxycodone in case your stomach acts up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I have that appointment for my kidneys on the 27th at noon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, blood work at 12, then see Dr. Patel at 12:30. Keep taking your lisinopril and amlodipine unless your blood pressure drops too low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor. I’m glad I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did the right thing. Take care, and call if anything changes before your appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this stay. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not good. Same as always—nauseous, stomach pain, can’t keep anything down. It feels like my usual flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned this feels like your typical gastroparesis episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. But this time there’s a burning in my upper belly, more than usual. It’s different. I’m just so tired of this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. That burning could be related to acid reflux. We’ll look into that. Your blood sugar was very high when you came in—691. They gave you insulin in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I didn’t know it was that high. Did that make me sicker?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: High blood sugar can definitely make gastroparesis worse. It slows digestion even more. We’re holding your sliding scale insulin for now and just giving your regular NPH to avoid lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Can I get something for pain? Dilaudid helps best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re avoiding Dilaudid because of your allergies. But we can give you oxycodone for now, and we’ll manage nausea with lorazepam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright… I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back. Your creatinine is up a bit—from your baseline of 1.6 to 2.0. But it’s coming down now, so your kidneys are likely just stressed from dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? My last admission they said I had kidney issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have stage III chronic kidney disease from diabetes. This was a temporary bump. We’re keeping you on lisinopril, which helps protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. And my blood pressure was high earlier—was that from the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. It’s improved now. We’re continuing your amlodipine and lisinopril. They’re safe with your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your stomach today? Any nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. I sipped some broth last night. The burning feeling is less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We think that burning might be from acid reflux—GERD. So we’ve started you on a medication called omeprazole twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Omeprazole? I’ve taken that before. Will it help prevent these flares?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might. If acid is triggering your gastroparesis, controlling it could reduce how often you get sick. Your primary doctor and GI specialist are on board with this plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so. I don’t want to keep coming back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re setting up a care plan with your PCP, psychiatrist, and social work to help prevent that. Your mental health plays a big role in these flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know… anxiety makes everything worse. But I feel stuck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not alone. The team met with you yesterday, and they’ll keep supporting you. We’re continuing your risperidone and mirtazapine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine test showed protein, which we expected due to diabetic kidney disease. But no infection—culture was negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no UTI? I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, no infection. The protein is from long-term diabetes effects. That’s why managing your blood sugar is so important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I try… but it’s hard when I’m sick and can’t eat regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. That’s why we’re simplifying your insulin—just your usual 70/30 with meals. No extra sliding scale unless we see a real need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Blood sugar is stable, and your creatinine dropped to 1.6. We’re going to advance your diet to soft foods today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. Can I try toast or crackers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, start small. We’ll watch how you tolerate it. Less nausea is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I ate half a banana and some applesauce. No vomiting!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent progress. Your body’s starting to reset. We’ll keep the oxycodone available if you need it, but you’re using it less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update: you’re much improved. Exam shows no abdominal pain, and you’re tolerating food. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Today? That’s fast. What about my blood sugar at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep monitoring your fingersticks like usual. If levels are too high or low, call your doctor. We’re sending you home with omeprazole twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds stay the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—amlodipine, lisinopril, insulin, lorazepam, mirtazapine, risperidone. All continue as before. Follow up with your PCP and psychiatrist soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll try to stick with the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. You’re stronger than you think. Take care, and call if anything worries you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still a little tired, but my stomach feels okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Your labs are improving, and you’re walking and eating—great signs. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home. Remember: omeprazole twice a day, monitor sugars, and call your team if you’re struggling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for listening this time. It means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’re on your side. Take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my hemoglobin test is still pending. Should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was ordered by your PCP for routine monitoring. No results yet, but nothing urgent. They’ll follow up with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I just get anxious when things are pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. That’s why your psychiatrist is staying involved. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you have your prescriptions, ride home, and follow-up appointments scheduled?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I have everything. I’ll call my doctor this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we hope not to see you back here soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same here. Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Rest well and keep in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling a bit emotional. This cycle is hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s okay to feel that way. You’re doing your best. The team is here to support you through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try to stay on track with the new medicine and my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we can ask. You’ve made real progress. Take it one step at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Patel. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You’re here for abdominal pain and nausea again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s the same as before—just like my gastroparesis flares. I was just discharged yesterday, but it came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’re saying it’s mostly nausea, vomiting, and belly pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. No diarrhea or fever, but I do feel some chest tightness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. We’ll check that out. Given your history of type 1 diabetes and gastroparesis, we want to make sure nothing serious is going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s not a heart attack or anything, right? I’m worried about the chest tightness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray just now, and it looks clear. No signs of infection, fluid, or heart enlargement. So it’s unlikely to be a lung or heart issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But my blood sugar must be high again, isn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was elevated when you arrived, but not as high as last time. We’re starting you on your regular insulin, adjusted for your current levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I hate when it gets too high. It makes the nausea worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Poor glucose control can definitely worsen gastroparesis. We’ll keep monitoring it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous. Haven’t kept anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you fluids and anti-nausea meds through the IV. We’re avoiding certain medications because of your allergies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I can’t take morphine or tramadol. What are you giving me instead?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re using ondansetron for nausea and a low dose of lorazepam to help with anxiety and nausea. Pain is being managed carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds safe. My kidneys are okay, right? I remember last time they were a little off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is stable now—stage 2 CKD, mild. We’re being cautious with fluids and meds to protect them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my eyes? I’ve been due for a retinal check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have background diabetic retinopathy, which means regular eye exams are important. We’ll remind your PCP to schedule that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugars are improving with the insulin adjustments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I try sipping water now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re going to start you on clear liquids. If you tolerate that, we’ll move to soft foods tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope this time it stays down. I’m so tired of being in and out of the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re working with your care team to help reduce these flares—your PCP, psychiatrist, and social work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well—kept down water and broth. We’re switching your insulin back to your home NPH regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I manage it better at home with my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Consistency helps prevent these flares. We’re also continuing omeprazole for acid reflux—it may be contributing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot I started that last time. Did it help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can help reduce stomach irritation. We’ll keep it going as part of your long-term plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on a soft diet now and still doing well. Nausea much better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. I even ate mashed potatoes yesterday!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great! Your labs are stable—kidneys, electrolytes, everything looks good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
